column2: Define a random variable, precisely.
column3: A function from the sample space to the real numbers: \(X: S \to \mathbb{R}\).

column2: Two dice are rolled. Give two different random variables on the same sample space.
column3: \(X\) = the sum, \(Y\) = the maximum. Both are functions on the 36 ordered pairs; for the outcome \((3,4)\), \(X = 7\) and \(Y = 4\).

column2: Where does the randomness in a random variable actually sit?
column3: In the outcome, not in the variable. The function is deterministic; which outcome occurred is what was uncertain.

column2: Define the PMF and the CDF of a discrete random variable, and say how they relate.
column3: \(p(x) = P(X = x)\) and \(F(x) = P(X \le x)\); the CDF is the running sum of the PMF.

column2: Two fair coins, \(X\) = number of heads. What are \(p(1)\) and \(F(1)\)?
column3: \(p(1) = 1/2\) (two of four outcomes) and \(F(1) = 3/4\) (everything up to and including 1).

column2: Name the three properties of a CDF.
column3: Nondecreasing, right-continuous, with limits 0 at \(-\infty\) and 1 at \(+\infty\).

column2: Given a CDF, how do you recover the PMF?
column3: Take the jump at each value: \(p(x) = F(x) - F(x^-)\), where \(F(x^-)\) is the limit from the left.

column2: What does i.i.d. commit you to, in two parts?
column3: Independence — the joint distribution factorises into a product — and identical distribution, the same PMF for every draw.

column2: Why does independence matter so much for a training loop?
column3: It factorises the joint likelihood into a product, so the log-likelihood is a sum that can be averaged over a minibatch.

column2: What are the mean and variance of a Bernoulli(\(p\)) variable, and where is the variance largest?
column3: Mean \(p\), variance \(p(1-p)\), maximised at \(p = 1/2\) where it is \(1/4\).

column2: State the fundamental bridge and explain in one line why it holds.
column3: \(P(A) = \mathbb{E}[1_A]\): the average of an indicator is the fraction of trials on which it is 1.

column2: Why does the Binomial PMF contain the factor \(\binom{n}{k}\)?
column3: It counts which \(k\) of the \(n\) trials succeeded; every such pattern has the same probability \(p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\).

column2: What are the mean and variance of \(\text{Bin}(10, 0.3)\)?
Write the Hypergeometric PMF for drawing \(k\) successes in \(n\) draws from a population of \(N\) containing \(K\) successes.
column3: \(\binom{K}{k}\binom{N-K}{n-k} \big/ \binom{N}{n}\).

column2: 5 tagged of 20 elk, catch 4. What is \(P(\text{exactly two tagged})\)?
When may you replace a Hypergeometric with a Binomial, and why?
column3: When the sample is a small fraction of the population — roughly under a tenth — so that removing items barely changes the success proportion and dependence is negligible.

column2: Write the Geometric PMF and derive it in one sentence.
column3: \((1-p)^{k-1}p\): the first \(k-1\) trials must fail and the \(k\)-th must succeed, and by independence the probabilities multiply.

column2: For a Geometric variable, what is \(P(X > n)\) and why?
column3: \((1-p)^n\): exceeding \(n\) means the first \(n\) trials all failed.

column2: With \(p = 0.2\), compute \(P(X = 3)\) and \(P(X > 5)\).
Why does the Negative Binomial carry \(\binom{k-1}{r-1}\) rather than \(\binom{k}{r}\)?
column3: The last trial is forced to be the \(r\)-th success, so the remaining \(r-1\) successes are placed among the first \(k-1\) trials.

column2: Write the Poisson PMF and give its mean and variance.
column3: \(p(k) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!\), with mean and variance both equal to \(\lambda\).

column2: What is the Poisson's generative story?
column3: The limit of \(\text{Bin}(n, \lambda/n)\) as \(n \to \infty\) with the mean held fixed — many independent chances, each individually very unlikely.

column2: For \(\lambda = 2\), what is \(P(X = 3)\)?
Which single limit supplies the \(e^{-\lambda}\) in the Poisson PMF?
column3: \((1 - \lambda/n)^n \to e^{-\lambda}\), from the \((1-p)^{n-k}\) factor of the Binomial.

column2: Which distribution is “trials until the \(r\)-th success”, and what is its mean?
column3: The Negative Binomial, with mean \(r/p\).

column2: Two distributions in the table have equal mean and variance. Which, and what does that symmetry cost you in practice?
column3: The Poisson, with both equal to \(\lambda\). Real count data is usually overdispersed (variance above the mean), so the Poisson understates the spread.

column2: What is the one-sentence story that identifies the Hypergeometric rather than the Binomial?
column3: Drawing without replacement — the success probability changes after each draw, so the trials are not independent.

column2: How does the categorical distribution relate to the discrete uniform?
column3: The uniform is the special case where every label has probability \(1/m\); the categorical allows arbitrary weights summing to one.

column2: Logits \((2, 1, 0)\). What is the categorical distribution at \(T = 0.5\)?
What two operations does top-\(k\) sampling perform, and which one is easy to forget?
column3: Truncate to the \(k\) largest weights, then renormalise to sum to one — the renormalisation is the step that is easy to forget.

column2: What distribution does a language model's final softmax define, and over what support?
column3: A categorical distribution over the vocabulary: one probability per token, summing to one across \(|V|\) entries.

column2: Why is temperature not a change to the model, but a change to the distribution?
column3: It divides the logits by \(T\) after the network has produced them and before the softmax, so the weights are unchanged and only the shape of the categorical PMF moves.

column2: A trajectory probability in RLHF is a product of categoricals. Which rule from essay one made that a product?
column3: The multiplication rule: the joint probability of a sequence of actions is the product of the conditional probabilities along the tree.

column2: Why is a negative log-likelihood loss usually a Gaussian, Bernoulli or categorical loss in disguise?
column3: Because each is \(-\log p(y \mid x)\) for one of those three output distributions: squared error for a Gaussian, binary cross-entropy for a Bernoulli, softmax cross-entropy for a categorical.
